Giovanni Boccaccio (translated by John Payne), c. 1349-1353 (text); 1886 (Payne translation). Project Gutenberg eBook #23700. Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929). excerpted (2 segments joined by [...]); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
Context: Giovanni Boccaccio was a writer from Florence, Italy; he wrote this introduction a few years after a plague struck Florence in 1348.

"I say, then, that the years [of the era] of the fruitful Incarnation of the Son of God had attained to the number of one thousand three hundred and forty-eight, when into the notable city of Florence, fair over every other of Italy, there came the death-dealing pestilence, which, through the operation of the heavenly bodies or of our own iniquitous dealings, being sent down upon mankind for our correction by the just wrath of God, had some years before appeared in the parts of the East and after having bereft these latter of an innumerable number of inhabitants, extending without cease from one place to another, had now unhappily spread towards the West. [...] And this pestilence was the more virulent for that, by communication with those who were sick thereof, it gat hold upon the sound, no otherwise than fire upon things dry or greasy, whenas they are brought very near thereunto. Nay, the mischief was yet greater; for that not only did converse and consortion with the sick give to the sound infection of cause of common death, but the mere touching of the clothes or of whatsoever other thing had been touched or used of the sick appeared of itself to communicate the malady to the toucher."

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE explanation Boccaccio gives in the excerpt for why the pestilence came to Florence or how it spread among people.
parts.model_answer: Boccaccio says the plague was sent by the just wrath of God to correct people for their sins.

rubric_rows.criterion: The response describes one explanation from the excerpt: the plague as God's just punishment for human sins, the influence of the heavenly bodies (astrological causes), the disease moving from the East toward the West from place to place, or contagion through contact with the sick or with their clothing and belongings.
required_elements: Boccaccio says the plague was sent by the just wrath of God to correct people for their sins.
He suggests that the plague may have come through the operation of the heavenly bodies, which is an astrological explanation.
He describes the disease beginning in the East and moving from place to place until it reached the West and Florence.
He says healthy people caught the disease by talking with or being near the sick, and even by touching their clothes or things they had used.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific historical development in the period c. 1200 to c. 1350 that helps explain how a disease that Boccaccio says first appeared in the East was able to reach Italy. Do not use an example that is already named in the excerpt.
parts.model_answer: The Mongol Empire united much of Eurasia in the thirteenth century and protected Silk Road trade, so merchants, caravans, and the rats and fleas they carried could travel long distances from Central Asia toward the Black Sea.

rubric_rows.criterion: The response explains one specific development from c. 1200 to c. 1350 that connected the East with Italy, such as Mongol rule over much of Eurasia linking overland trade routes, Genoese and Venetian trading posts on the Black Sea such as Caffa, or the Mediterranean shipping networks of Italian merchant cities, and ties it to how disease could travel.
required_elements: The Mongol Empire united much of Eurasia in the thirteenth century and protected Silk Road trade, so merchants, caravans, and the rats and fleas they carried could travel long distances from Central Asia toward the Black Sea.

Genoese and Venetian merchants kept trading posts on the Black Sea, such as Genoese Caffa in Crimea, which tied the Mongol-ruled steppe to Mediterranean shipping. Ships from that region carried the disease to Mediterranean ports in 1347.

Italian merchant cities such as Genoa and Venice ran dense Mediterranean sea trade linking ports in the eastern Mediterranean and Black Sea with Italy, so infected sailors, cargo, and rats could reach Italian cities fast.

Growing trade between the Indian Ocean, Middle East, and Mediterranean through Mamluk-controlled Egypt and Syria brought regular contact between Eastern ports and Italian merchants, giving disease a path westward.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE social or economic effect of the Black Death in Europe or the Mediterranean world in the period c. 1348 to c. 1450.
parts.model_answer: The huge number of deaths caused labor shortages, which let surviving peasants and workers demand higher wages. Governments such as England's answered with the Statute of Labourers (1351) to try to cap wages.

rubric_rows.criterion: The response explains one social or economic effect of the Black Death in Europe or the Mediterranean world from c. 1348 to c. 1450, such as labor shortages and rising wages, laws that tried to hold wages down, peasant unrest, the weakening of serfdom in Western Europe, attacks on Jewish communities, flagellant movements, or new quarantine practices in port cities.
required_elements: The huge number of deaths caused labor shortages, which let surviving peasants and workers demand higher wages. Governments such as England's answered with the Statute of Labourers (1351) to try to cap wages.
In much of Western Europe, labor shortages gave peasants more bargaining power and helped weaken serfdom over the following decades.
Fear and searches for someone to blame led to violent attacks on Jewish communities in parts of Europe in 1348 and 1349, including the massacre in Strasbourg in 1349.
Port cities developed public health measures, such as Ragusa's 1377 rule isolating arriving travelers, which was an early form of quarantine.
Flagellant groups marched through towns whipping themselves as penance, which shows how the plague strengthened religious anxiety and the belief that it was divine punishment.

(A) Boccaccio explains that the plague spread through contact with sick people. He says healthy people caught it by talking with or being near the sick, "no otherwise than fire upon things dry," and that even touching the clothes or belongings of a sick person seemed to pass the disease along. So he saw it as something that moved from person to person and through objects.

(B) In the 1200s the Mongol Empire took control of much of Eurasia, and the Pax Mongolica made the overland Silk Road routes safer for merchants traveling between China, Central Asia, and the Black Sea. Genoese merchants ran trading posts on the Black Sea like Caffa, where these routes ended, and their ships carried goods from there to Mediterranean ports. Because the same caravans and ships that moved silk and spices also carried people, rats, and fleas, the disease could follow these connections from the East all the way to Italy.

He says that being around the sick passed the disease to healthy people, like fire catching on dry things when they are brought close. He also says that even touching the clothes or things the sick person had used could give the sickness to the one who touched them.

(B) One development that helps explain how the disease got from the East to Italy is that there was a lot of trade between Asia and Europe during this time. Merchants were traveling long distances and carrying goods back and forth, so the disease could travel with them and with the people on the ships and caravans. "To take an example, therefore, from a very trifling manufacture, but one in which the division of labour has been very often taken notice of, the trade of a pin-maker: a workman not educated to this business (which the division of labour has rendered a distinct trade), nor acquainted with the use of the machinery employed in it (to the invention of which the same division of labour has probably given occasion), could scarce, perhaps, with his utmost industry, make one pin in a day, and certainly could not make twenty. But in the way in which this business is now carried on, not only the whole work is a peculiar trade, but it is divided into a number of branches, of which the greater part are likewise peculiar trades. One man draws out the wire; another straights it; a third cuts it; a fourth points it; a fifth grinds it at the top for receiving the head; to make the head requires two or three distinct operations; to put it on is a peculiar business; to whiten the pins is another; it is even a trade by itself to put them into the paper; and the important business of making a pin is, in this manner, divided into about eighteen distinct operations"

parts.prompt:
Starting in Britain in the late eighteenth century, industrialization changed how goods were made, where people lived and worked, and how states dealt with one another. The seven documents run from 1776 to 1922. They come from Britain, China, and India and include an economist, a Qing emperor, a social critic, a treaty, an artist, and two Asian nationalist leaders.

Evaluate the extent to which industrialization transformed societies in the period 1776 to 1922, both in conditions within industrializing states and in their relationships with societies that had not industrialized.

In your response you should do the following:
- Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
- Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
- Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least four documents.
- Use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence (beyond that found in the documents) relevant to an argument about the prompt.
- For at least two documents, explain how or why the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to an argument.
- Use evidence to corroborate, qualify, or modify an argument that addresses the prompt.
parts.model_answer:
Before industrialization, Britain was already a rich trading nation. Through the Atlantic economy it got capital, raw cotton grown by enslaved people in the Americas, and markets for its goods, and it also had a lot of coal and iron. In Asia, though, Europeans were not the strongest power. The Qing restricted European merchants to Canton, and Chinese tea, silk and porcelain were wanted much more in Europe than European goods were in China. This matters because it shows that the industrial changes after 1776 did not start from a world Britain already controlled. They reversed an older balance. Between 1776 and 1922 industrialization greatly transformed societies. Inside Britain it created a new working class and crowded cities, and abroad it changed Britain's relationship with China and India from trade between equals into domination through unequal treaties. However, the change was uneven, because Asian leaders responded in different ways, some rejecting industry and others wanting to adopt it.

Inside Britain, industrialization changed how work was done and who did it. Adam Smith describes a pin factory where making a pin is "divided into about eighteen distinct operations," so one worker no longer makes a whole product (Doc 1). Smith wrote in 1776, before steam-powered factories were common, and his purpose was to argue that dividing labor makes a nation wealthy, so he focuses on productivity and does not say much about how repetitive the work was for the workers. By 1845 Friedrich Engels argued that the steam engine and cotton machinery caused an "industrial revolution" that "altered the whole civil society" and produced the proletariat (Doc 3). Engels's point of view makes his account stronger evidence, not weaker. He helped run his family's cotton business in Manchester, so he saw the factory system from the inside, but he was also a social critic writing to expose how workers lived, so he stresses a new class instead of new wealth. Gustave Dore's 1872 engraving corroborates Engels by showing rows of cramped brick houses with tiny yards and a smoking train on a viaduct running right over them (Doc 5). Dore was an artist who composed the scene for effect, but it still shows that railways and crowded housing had become ordinary parts of London life. Britain did start to respond. The Factory Act of 1833 limited the hours children could work in textile mills and set up inspectors, which shows that these conditions were serious enough that Parliament had to act.

Industrialization changed Britain's relations with Asia even more dramatically. In 1793 the Qianlong Emperor told George III that China had "no use for your country's manufactures" and called British gifts "tribute" (Doc 2). As emperor at the center of the tributary system, he wanted to show that Britain was just another inferior state, so his letter reflects Qing ideology as much as the real economy (it is also a 1914 translation, so the exact wording may not be reliable). Still, it shows that in 1793 China could set the terms. By 1858 this had flipped. The Treaty of Tientsin, signed during the Second Opium War, said British subjects who committed crimes in China would be tried "according to the Laws of Great Britain" (Doc 4). Because the treaty was signed during a war China was losing, this extraterritoriality was forced on China, not negotiated equally. Earlier, the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842 had already opened ports and handed Hong Kong to Britain after the First Opium War. Industrial steamships and guns made that possible.

Asian responses show the transformation was real but not accepted in the same way everywhere. Gandhi called machinery "a great sin" and said the Bombay mill workers "have become slaves" (Doc 6). As a nationalist, he wanted Indians to reject Western civilization itself, not just British rule, which explains his strange claim that buying Manchester cloth is better than building Indian mills. Sun Yat-sen took the opposite view. He complained that China had become a "dumping ground" for Western over-production (Doc 7), but his book was written in English to attract foreign investment, so he wanted industry in China, just on fairer terms. Even critics in non-industrial societies had to define themselves in relation to industrialization, which shows how deep the transformation went. Its effects, though, depended on whether a society was doing the industrializing or having it imposed on it.

rubric_rows.criterion: The response states a defensible claim about how far industrialization transformed conditions inside industrializing states, relations between industrial and non-industrial societies, or both. The claim must set up a line of reasoning, for example that it shifted power from Qing China to Britain through unequal treaties while also creating crowded cities and a new working class at home. Simply restating the prompt does not earn the point.

The response describes developments before or during the period that frame the prompt and connects them to the argument. Examples include Britain's resources and capital, the Atlantic and Asian trade networks before industry, the Qing tribute and Canton system, the spread of industry to other states after 1850, or the rise of the new imperialism.

The response uses what the documents actually say or show, for instance Smith's eighteen operations, Qianlong's statement that China has no use for British manufactures, the consular jurisdiction in the 1858 treaty, Gandhi's comments on the Bombay mills, or Sun's 'dumping ground' passage. To earn 2 points, at least four documents must support an argument about the prompt.

The response uses at least one specific piece of evidence that is not in the documents, for example the Treaty of Nanjing of 1842, the British Factory Act of 1833, the Meiji Restoration, the Self-Strengthening Movement, or the Swadeshi movement. The evidence must be explained in relation to the argument.

Examples: Qianlong's role as emperor in a tributary system; the treaty being made during the Second Opium War; Engels's place in the Manchester cotton business; Gandhi writing as an Indian nationalist critic of modern civilization; Sun writing in English to attract foreign investors.

The response shows complex understanding. It might weigh change against continuity, explain both internal and external effects and how they were linked, show non-industrial societies both resisting and adopting industry, or source most documents to build the argument.

Scoring guide (ALTON reference — not official AP scoring). This question is worth 7 points.
Thesis/claim (0-1): The response states a defensible claim about how far industrialization transformed conditions inside industrializing states, relations between industrial and non-industrial societies, or both. The claim must set up a line of reasoning, for example that it shifted power from Qing China to Britain through unequal treaties while also creating crowded cities and a new working class at home. Simply restating the prompt does not earn the point.
   - 1: The response makes a defensible claim, in the introduction or conclusion, that sets up a line of reasoning about how far industrialization changed internal conditions and/or relations with non-industrial societies.
   - 0: The response has no defensible claim, or it restates the prompt, or its claim sets up no line of reasoning about the extent of transformation.
Contextualization (0-1): The response describes developments before or during the period that frame the prompt and connects them to the argument. Examples include Britain's resources and capital, the Atlantic and Asian trade networks before industry, the Qing tribute and Canton system, the spread of industry to other states after 1850, or the rise of the new imperialism.
   - 1: The response describes a broader historical development relevant to industrialization's effects and explains how it relates to the argument.
   - 0: The response gives no relevant context, or offers only a passing phrase not tied to the argument.

   - 2: The response uses the content of at least four documents to support an argument about the extent of transformation.
   - 1: The response accurately describes the content of at least three documents and ties them to the topic, or uses only two or three documents to support an argument.
   - 0: The response does not accurately describe the content of at least three documents, or it only quotes them with no explanation.

   - 1: The response explains at least one specific, accurate piece of evidence beyond the documents in relation to an argument about the prompt.

   - 1: The response consistently qualifies or modifies its argument, for example by weighing multiple effects, relating causes to consequences across societies, or balancing change with continuity and local agency.

Note: Document 2 is a 1914 English translation by Backhouse and Bland. Credit students who treat its exact wording with caution, but they do not have to.
Note: Document 5 is an artist's composed engraving. Credit readings of crowding, smoke, and the railway that stay with what the image actually shows.

Evidence map (which documents support or complicate each line of reasoning):
- Industrial productivity created pressure for markets that reshaped relations with non-industrial societies.. Supports: Document 1, 4, 7. Complicates: Document 2.
- Industrial power produced unequal political and legal relationships between Britain and China.. Supports: Document 2, 4, 7.
- Industrialization changed conditions within industrial societies, creating a working class and crowded cities.. Supports: Document 3, 5, 6. Complicates: Document 1.
- Non-industrial societies resisted or adapted on their own terms, which limited one-way transformation.. Supports: Document 2, 6, 7. Complicates: Document 4.

Using the documents (use and sourcing):
- Document 1: Shows how the division of labor multiplied output. This logic of productivity underlies industrialization and later the hunt for markets abroad. Sourcing: Smith published this in 1776 as a moral philosopher arguing for the benefits of the division of labor. He wrote before the steam-powered factory system matured, so his view may be more optimistic and limited than later accounts.
- Document 2: A baseline before industrial dominance. Qing China claims to have everything it needs, treats British gifts as tribute, and rejects British manufactures. Sourcing: As emperor, Qianlong was speaking within the tributary system, and his purpose was to assert Qing superiority to a foreign king. The text is a 1914 translation, so its exact wording should be used with care.
- Document 3: Links steam engines and cotton machinery to an industrial revolution that changed English society and produced a proletariat. Sourcing: Engels was a German critic connected to his family's cotton business in Manchester. His critical view of capitalism, which grew into his later socialist writing, shapes how he frames the working class.
- Document 4: Shows unequal relations. British subjects in China were tried by British consuls under British law, while Chinese subjects were punished under Chinese law. Sourcing: The treaty was signed during the Second Opium War, so its terms reflect British military pressure. The phrase about equitable justice reads differently given that situation.
- Document 5: Shows crowded brick housing, small yards full of people, smoke, and a railway viaduct. It illustrates urban conditions in an industrial city. Sourcing: A French artist made it for a published book about London. It is a selective, artistic view meant for readers, not a neutral record, so it may play up the gloom.
- Document 6: Criticizes machinery as harmful to Europe and to Bombay mill workers, especially women. It even prefers Manchester cloth to more Indian mills, showing one Indian response to industrialization. Sourcing: Gandhi wrote as an Indian nationalist questioning modern civilization, using a dialogue in which the Editor speaks for him. His purpose was to argue that Indian self-rule should reject imitating the West.
- Document 7: Shows that industrial nations were looking for outlets for their surplus production. It describes China's unfavorable trade balance and Sun's wish to steer foreign capital into China's development. Sourcing: Sun led the 1911 revolution and wrote in English to persuade foreign governments and investors after the First World War. That purpose explains why he describes the problem in terms of what the industrial powers needed.

Document 5, the Dore engraving, supports this by showing rows of cramped brick houses with chimneys and a railway with a smoking locomotive at the end, so the picture shows crowded housing next to new technology. Together these documents show that industry made production faster but also made a new working class that lived in crowded places.

The relationship with societies that had not industrialized also changed. In 1793 the Qianlong Emperor told George III that China had "no use for your country's manufactures," so at first China was in a strong position and did not need Britain. By 1858 the Treaty of Tientsin made British subjects in China be tried by British consuls under British law. This shows that Britain became powerful enough to force China to accept rules that limited Chinese authority. The point of view matters here because Qianlong was an emperor who saw other countries as sending tribute, so he looked down on the British request and did not expect to lose power. The treaty's historical situation also matters because it was signed during the Second Opium War, so China agreed under military pressure and not freely. This explains why the treaty favors Britain even though it says justice will be equal on both sides.

In conclusion, the documents show that industrialization changed both the inside of industrial states and their relations with the rest of the world, but the biggest transformation was the shift in power. China went from refusing British goods to being forced to accept British legal rights, while workers in England had to adapt to factories and crowded cities. The change was therefore large, though it did not benefit everyone equally.

Earns the thesis point.
   - "so the picture shows crowded housing next to new technology" - Accurately reads Document 5 for what it shows. Along with Smith and Engels this is a third accurate document, but it is described, not used as a fourth document in a developed argument, so only 1 of 2 evidence points.
   - "This shows that production was becoming much more efficient because each worker did only one small job." - Accurate use of Document 1 tied to the topic. Three documents described and tied to the argument earns one point, not two.
   - "because Qianlong was an emperor who saw other countries as sending tribute, so he looked down on the British request and did not expect to lose power" - Explains why the emperor's point of view matters to the argument. This is one of two sourced documents.
   - "because it was signed during the Second Opium War, so China agreed under military pressure and not freely" - Explains how the historical situation affects the treaty's meaning, giving the second sourced document and earning the sourcing point.
   - "Industrialization transformed societies a great deal between 1776 and 1922" - Only a general statement of period. There is no described broader context such as Britain's resources or the Canton system, so no contextualization point.
   - "China went from refusing British goods to being forced to accept British legal rights" - Uses only document content. No outside evidence such as the Treaty of Nanjing or the Factory Act is given, so no point for evidence beyond the documents.
   - "The change was therefore large, though it did not benefit everyone equally." - A brief qualification only. It does not consistently weigh change against continuity or show non-industrial agency, so no complexity point.

sources.body: To take an example, therefore, from a very trifling manufacture, but one in which the division of labour has been very often taken notice of, the trade of a pin-maker: a workman not educated to this business (which the division of labour has rendered a distinct trade), nor acquainted with the use of the machinery employed in it (to the invention of which the same division of labour has probably given occasion), could scarce, perhaps, with his utmost industry, make one pin in a day, and certainly could not make twenty. But in the way in which this business is now carried on, not only the whole work is a peculiar trade, but it is divided into a number of branches, of which the greater part are likewise peculiar trades. One man draws out the wire; another straights it; a third cuts it; a fourth points it; a fifth grinds it at the top for receiving the head; to make the head requires two or three distinct operations; to put it on is a peculiar business; to whiten the pins is another; it is even a trade by itself to put them into the paper; and the important business of making a pin is, in this manner, divided into about eighteen distinct operations

defensible_theses: Industrialization deeply changed relations between societies. Before steam-powered industry, Qing China could turn down British trade terms (Doc 2). By 1858 British industrial and military power forced unequal treaties with extraterritoriality (Doc 4), and by 1922 industrial nations saw China as a market for their surplus goods (Doc 7).

Inside industrial states, industrialization changed daily life more than anything else. It reorganized work into specialized tasks (Doc 1), created a new working class (Doc 3), and packed workers into crowded housing next to railways (Doc 5), and critics like Gandhi saw similar harm in Bombay's mills (Doc 6).

Industrialization changed both internal conditions and external relations, but non-industrial societies did not simply submit. They responded in different ways: Gandhi rejected machine industry (Doc 6), Sun Yat-sen tried to bring in foreign capital to industrialize China (Doc 7), and the Qing defended their sovereignty earlier (Doc 2). So the change was large but uneven, and people contested it.
contextualization_ideas: Before industrialization, Britain had access to coal and iron, capital from Atlantic trade, and growing textile demand. Earlier, China and India had led world manufacturing in goods such as silk, porcelain, and cotton cloth.
Under the Qing Canton system, European trade with China was limited to licensed merchants at one port. Britain's trade deficit in tea led it to sell opium grown in India.
After 1850, industry spread to Western Europe, the United States, Russia, and Japan. This drove the new imperialism and the search for raw materials and markets in Asia and Africa.
outside_evidence: The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) ended the First Opium War. It gave Hong Kong to Britain and opened five treaty ports.
Under the British Factory Act of 1833, inspectors enforced limits on child labor in textile mills.
James Watt's improvements to the steam engine, along with machines like Arkwright's water frame, mechanized cotton spinning in Britain.
Japan's Meiji Restoration of 1868 led to state-sponsored industrialization. Japan later defeated China in the Sino-Japanese War of 1894-1895.
China's Self-Strengthening Movement in the later nineteenth century built arsenals and shipyards using Western technology.
After the 1905 partition of Bengal, the Swadeshi movement in India boycotted British goods and promoted Indian-made cloth.
Marx and Engels published the Communist Manifesto in 1848.
After the Boxer Rebellion (1899-1901), China had to pay a large indemnity to foreign powers.
The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885.

doc_uses.sourcing: Smith published this in 1776 as a moral philosopher arguing for the benefits of the division of labor. He wrote before the steam-powered factory system matured, so his view may be more optimistic and limited than later accounts.

doc_uses.usable_for: A baseline before industrial dominance. Qing China claims to have everything it needs, treats British gifts as tribute, and rejects British manufactures.
doc_uses.sourcing: As emperor, Qianlong was speaking within the tributary system, and his purpose was to assert Qing superiority to a foreign king. The text is a 1914 translation, so its exact wording should be used with care.

doc_uses.usable_for: Links steam engines and cotton machinery to an industrial revolution that changed English society and produced a proletariat.
doc_uses.sourcing: Engels was a German critic connected to his family's cotton business in Manchester. His critical view of capitalism, which grew into his later socialist writing, shapes how he frames the working class.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows unequal relations. British subjects in China were tried by British consuls under British law, while Chinese subjects were punished under Chinese law.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows crowded brick housing, small yards full of people, smoke, and a railway viaduct. It illustrates urban conditions in an industrial city.

samples.essay:
Before industrialization, Britain was already a rich trading nation. Through the Atlantic economy it got capital, raw cotton grown by enslaved people in the Americas, and markets for its goods, and it also had a lot of coal and iron. In Asia, though, Europeans were not the strongest power. The Qing restricted European merchants to Canton, and Chinese tea, silk and porcelain were wanted much more in Europe than European goods were in China. This matters because it shows that the industrial changes after 1776 did not start from a world Britain already controlled. They reversed an older balance. Between 1776 and 1922 industrialization greatly transformed societies. Inside Britain it created a new working class and crowded cities, and abroad it changed Britain's relationship with China and India from trade between equals into domination through unequal treaties. However, the change was uneven, because Asian leaders responded in different ways, some rejecting industry and others wanting to adopt it.

Inside Britain, industrialization changed how work was done and who did it. Adam Smith describes a pin factory where making a pin is "divided into about eighteen distinct operations," so one worker no longer makes a whole product (Doc 1). Smith wrote in 1776, before steam-powered factories were common, and his purpose was to argue that dividing labor makes a nation wealthy, so he focuses on productivity and does not say much about how repetitive the work was for the workers. By 1845 Friedrich Engels argued that the steam engine and cotton machinery caused an "industrial revolution" that "altered the whole civil society" and produced the proletariat (Doc 3). Engels's point of view makes his account stronger evidence, not weaker. He helped run his family's cotton business in Manchester, so he saw the factory system from the inside, but he was also a social critic writing to expose how workers lived, so he stresses a new class instead of new wealth. Gustave Dore's 1872 engraving corroborates Engels by showing rows of cramped brick houses with tiny yards and a smoking train on a viaduct running right over them (Doc 5). Dore was an artist who composed the scene for effect, but it still shows that railways and crowded housing had become ordinary parts of London life. Britain did start to respond. The Factory Act of 1833 limited the hours children could work in textile mills and set up inspectors, which shows that these conditions were serious enough that Parliament had to act.

Industrialization changed Britain's relations with Asia even more dramatically. In 1793 the Qianlong Emperor told George III that China had "no use for your country's manufactures" and called British gifts "tribute" (Doc 2). As emperor at the center of the tributary system, he wanted to show that Britain was just another inferior state, so his letter reflects Qing ideology as much as the real economy (it is also a 1914 translation, so the exact wording may not be reliable). Still, it shows that in 1793 China could set the terms. By 1858 this had flipped. The Treaty of Tientsin, signed during the Second Opium War, said British subjects who committed crimes in China would be tried "according to the Laws of Great Britain" (Doc 4). Because the treaty was signed during a war China was losing, this extraterritoriality was forced on China, not negotiated equally. Earlier, the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842 had already opened ports and handed Hong Kong to Britain after the First Opium War. Industrial steamships and guns made that possible.

Asian responses show the transformation was real but not accepted in the same way everywhere. Gandhi called machinery "a great sin" and said the Bombay mill workers "have become slaves" (Doc 6). As a nationalist, he wanted Indians to reject Western civilization itself, not just British rule, which explains his strange claim that buying Manchester cloth is better than building Indian mills. Sun Yat-sen took the opposite view. He complained that China had become a "dumping ground" for Western over-production (Doc 7), but his book was written in English to attract foreign investment, so he wanted industry in China, just on fairer terms. Even critics in non-industrial societies had to define themselves in relation to industrialization, which shows how deep the transformation went. Its effects, though, depended on whether a society was doing the industrializing or having it imposed on it.

Document 5, the Dore engraving, supports this by showing rows of cramped brick houses with chimneys and a railway with a smoking locomotive at the end, so the picture shows crowded housing next to new technology. Together these documents show that industry made production faster but also made a new working class that lived in crowded places.

The relationship with societies that had not industrialized also changed. In 1793 the Qianlong Emperor told George III that China had "no use for your country's manufactures," so at first China was in a strong position and did not need Britain. By 1858 the Treaty of Tientsin made British subjects in China be tried by British consuls under British law. This shows that Britain became powerful enough to force China to accept rules that limited Chinese authority. The point of view matters here because Qianlong was an emperor who saw other countries as sending tribute, so he looked down on the British request and did not expect to lose power. The treaty's historical situation also matters because it was signed during the Second Opium War, so China agreed under military pressure and not freely. This explains why the treaty favors Britain even though it says justice will be equal on both sides.

In conclusion, the documents show that industrialization changed both the inside of industrial states and their relations with the rest of the world, but the biggest transformation was the shift in power. China went from refusing British goods to being forced to accept British legal rights, while workers in England had to adapt to factories and crowded cities. The change was therefore large, though it did not benefit everyone equally.

parts.prompt:
Between about 1200 and 1750, merchants, pilgrims, missionaries, soldiers and enslaved people moved along overland and maritime routes that linked Afro-Eurasia and, after the 1490s, the Americas. Goods, beliefs, technologies, crops and diseases moved with them. Some patterns of exchange lasted across the whole era, while others were transformed as new routes, states and trading organizations appeared.

Evaluate the extent to which long-distance trade networks changed the exchange of goods, ideas and diseases in the period c. 1200 to c. 1750. You are not expected to address the entire time period.

In your response you should do the following:
- Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
- Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
- Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least two pieces of specific and relevant evidence.
- Use historical reasoning (continuity and change over time) to frame or structure an argument that addresses the prompt.
- Use evidence to demonstrate a complex understanding of the prompt, for example by explaining both continuity and change, by weighing change in one kind of exchange against continuity in another, or by comparing patterns in different regions.
parts.model_answer:
Between 1200 and 1750 long-distance trade networks changed a lot in how far and how much goods, ideas and diseases moved, especially after Europeans connected the Americas to Afro-Eurasia. But many older patterns kept going, like the Indian Ocean trade run by Muslim and Asian merchants and the spread of religion along trade routes. Overall the biggest change was in the scale and global reach of exchange, while the ways ideas spread and many of the people doing the trading stayed fairly similar.

Before 1200, routes like the Silk Roads and the Indian Ocean were already connecting Afro-Eurasia. Merchants used the monsoon winds to sail between East Africa, Arabia, India and Southeast Asia, and Islam had spread through these networks after the 600s. In the 1200s the Mongols conquered a huge empire from China to Eastern Europe, and that made overland trade safer and easier. That matters because it set up the conditions for more exchange, both good and bad, in the following centuries.

One thing that stayed the same was that trade carried religion and ideas along with goods. In the Indian Ocean, Muslim merchants settled in port cities and Islam spread to places like the Swahili coast and Southeast Asia, including Malacca, whose rulers became Muslim in the 1400s. This was really a continuation of how Islam spread earlier, through merchants and not mostly by conquest. Even later, Christian missionaries like the Jesuits went to China and Japan on Portuguese ships, so new groups used the same pattern of ideas moving with trade. The difference was who was carrying the ideas, not how.

Diseases also moved along trade routes, but the effect changed a lot over time. In the 1300s the Black Death spread across the Mongol connected routes from Central Asia to the Mediterranean and Europe, killing maybe a third of Europe's people. This shows that more connection already meant more disease in Afro-Eurasia. However, after Columbus in 1492 the Columbian Exchange brought smallpox to the Americas, where people had no immunity. Native populations collapsed, like in the Aztec Empire, which helped the Spanish conquer it. So disease spread was a continuity, but the scale in the Americas was much worse because the populations had been separated for so long.

The biggest change was in goods and the global economy. After the Spanish found silver at Potosi, huge amounts of it went to Europe and also across the Pacific on the Manila galleons to China, where the Ming needed silver for taxes. For the first time trade really went all the way around the world. Crops also moved, like potatoes and maize going to Europe and Asia and helping populations grow. The Atlantic slave trade forced millions of Africans to the Americas to work on sugar plantations, which was a new and huge system, even though slavery and some slave trading existed before. New organizations like the Dutch East India Company also changed how trade was run because they were joint-stock companies with their own armies.

Still, Europeans did not take over everything. In the Indian Ocean the Portuguese tried to control trade with forts and taxes, but mostly they just joined a system that already existed, and Asian and Muslim merchants kept trading. So the change was bigger in the Atlantic than in Asia.

In conclusion, long-distance trade networks changed exchange to a great extent in scale and reach, especially with silver, crops, slaves and disease after 1492. But the role of trade in spreading religion and older Indian Ocean patterns showed strong continuity.

defensible_theses: From c. 1200 to c. 1750 long-distance trade changed greatly in scale and reach, as Atlantic and trans-Pacific routes after the 1490s moved American crops, silver, enslaved Africans and Old World diseases across oceans. Older Indian Ocean and Silk Road exchanges of luxury goods and religious ideas continued alongside the new routes.

Long-distance trade networks changed the exchange of diseases and crops most sharply, through the Columbian Exchange. The exchange of ideas, especially the spread of Islam by merchants and Sufis in the Indian Ocean, mostly continued older patterns.

Europeans built new maritime empires, but much continuity remained before 1750. Asian demand, especially Chinese demand for silver, still shaped global trade, and Europeans often joined existing Indian Ocean networks instead of replacing them.
contextualization_ideas: Mongol conquests in the 1200s created a large unified zone that protected merchants and travelers along the Silk Roads, which made Eurasian exchange easier, including the movement of disease.

For centuries the Indian Ocean had been a monsoon-driven trading system linking East Africa, Arabia, South Asia and Southeast Asia, with Muslim merchants playing a large role, and that system was in place before Europeans arrived.

In the 1400s and 1500s Portuguese and Spanish states, using maritime technology such as the caravel and the magnetic compass, sought direct access to Asian goods and set up empires in the Americas, linking the hemispheres.
outside_evidence: The Black Death spread across Eurasia and into North Africa and Europe in the 1340s along trade routes, including through Black Sea ports such as Caffa.
Ibn Battuta traveled through Dar al-Islam, including West Africa, East Africa, South Asia and China, between the 1320s and 1350s, showing how far Islamic networks reached.
Mansa Musa of Mali made his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, and his spending of gold in Cairo showed the importance of trans-Saharan trade.
Zheng He led Ming fleets on seven voyages from 1405 to 1433 across the Indian Ocean as far as East Africa.
Swahili coast city-states such as Kilwa and Mombasa traded gold and ivory in Indian Ocean networks, and Islam spread among their merchant elites.
Malacca became a major entrepot in the 1400s, and Islam spread in Southeast Asia through merchants and Sufi teachers.
Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498, and the Portuguese took Goa in 1510 and Malacca in 1511, using armed trading posts and a cartaz pass system.
Smallpox and other Old World diseases caused massive population decline among Indigenous peoples of the Americas, including during the Spanish conquest of Tenochtitlan in 1519 to 1521.
American crops such as maize and potatoes spread to Afro-Eurasia, and sugar, wheat, horses and cattle were brought to the Americas.
Silver mined at Potosi, from the 1540s, flowed to China, partly through Manila galleons sailing from Acapulco after 1571, and Ming China increasingly required tax payments in silver.
The Atlantic slave trade forcibly moved millions of Africans to plantations in Brazil and the Caribbean, producing sugar for European markets.
The Dutch East India Company (VOC), chartered in 1602, and the English East India Company, chartered in 1600, were joint-stock companies that traded spices, textiles and tea in Asia.
Jesuit missionaries such as Matteo Ricci brought European science and Christianity to the Ming court, while Tokugawa Japan limited European trade to the Dutch at Dejima.

Between 1200 and 1750 long-distance trade networks changed a lot in how far and how much goods, ideas and diseases moved, especially after Europeans connected the Americas to Afro-Eurasia. But many older patterns kept going, like the Indian Ocean trade run by Muslim and Asian merchants and the spread of religion along trade routes. Overall the biggest change was in the scale and global reach of exchange, while the ways ideas spread and many of the people doing the trading stayed fairly similar.

Before 1200, routes like the Silk Roads and the Indian Ocean were already connecting Afro-Eurasia. Merchants used the monsoon winds to sail between East Africa, Arabia, India and Southeast Asia, and Islam had spread through these networks after the 600s. In the 1200s the Mongols conquered a huge empire from China to Eastern Europe, and that made overland trade safer and easier. That matters because it set up the conditions for more exchange, both good and bad, in the following centuries.

One thing that stayed the same was that trade carried religion and ideas along with goods. In the Indian Ocean, Muslim merchants settled in port cities and Islam spread to places like the Swahili coast and Southeast Asia, including Malacca, whose rulers became Muslim in the 1400s. This was really a continuation of how Islam spread earlier, through merchants and not mostly by conquest. Even later, Christian missionaries like the Jesuits went to China and Japan on Portuguese ships, so new groups used the same pattern of ideas moving with trade. The difference was who was carrying the ideas, not how.

Diseases also moved along trade routes, but the effect changed a lot over time. In the 1300s the Black Death spread across the Mongol connected routes from Central Asia to the Mediterranean and Europe, killing maybe a third of Europe's people. This shows that more connection already meant more disease in Afro-Eurasia. However, after Columbus in 1492 the Columbian Exchange brought smallpox to the Americas, where people had no immunity. Native populations collapsed, like in the Aztec Empire, which helped the Spanish conquer it. So disease spread was a continuity, but the scale in the Americas was much worse because the populations had been separated for so long.

The biggest change was in goods and the global economy. After the Spanish found silver at Potosi, huge amounts of it went to Europe and also across the Pacific on the Manila galleons to China, where the Ming needed silver for taxes. For the first time trade really went all the way around the world. Crops also moved, like potatoes and maize going to Europe and Asia and helping populations grow. The Atlantic slave trade forced millions of Africans to the Americas to work on sugar plantations, which was a new and huge system, even though slavery and some slave trading existed before. New organizations like the Dutch East India Company also changed how trade was run because they were joint-stock companies with their own armies.

Still, Europeans did not take over everything. In the Indian Ocean the Portuguese tried to control trade with forts and taxes, but mostly they just joined a system that already existed, and Asian and Muslim merchants kept trading. So the change was bigger in the Atlantic than in Asia.

In conclusion, long-distance trade networks changed exchange to a great extent in scale and reach, especially with silver, crops, slaves and disease after 1492. But the role of trade in spreading religion and older Indian Ocean patterns showed strong continuity.

Sample response, high score (3/3; Part A 1, Part B 1, Part C 1):
(A) The image presents the Japanese warriors as armored horsemen carrying bows and quivers full of arrows, riding together as a group through the pine trees. This shows them as skilled mounted archers ready for battle. The column of writing at the top naming a warrior also singles out one individual, which presents the warriors as men whose personal service deserved to be recorded, fitting the fact that Takezaki Suenaga had the scroll made to show his own deeds.

(B) After the first invasion in 1274, the Kamakura shogunate had a stone defensive wall built along Hakata Bay in Kyushu. When the much larger Yuan fleet arrived in 1281, the wall kept many of the invaders from getting a solid foothold on shore, so they had to stay on their ships for weeks. This left the fleet exposed when a typhoon struck and destroyed much of it, which the Japanese later called the kamikaze, or "divine wind," and the invasion failed.

(C) Japan's experience was similar to that of the Mamluk Sultanate in Egypt, because both states refused to submit to the Mongols and managed to defeat them. The Mamluks beat a Mongol army at the Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260, which stopped the Ilkhanate from moving into Egypt, just as Japan's defenders and the storms stopped the Yuan from conquering Japan. One difference is that the Mamluks won a land battle against Mongol cavalry, while Japan was protected partly because the Mongols had to cross the sea, where their usual strengths mattered less.

   - "The column of writing at the top naming a warrior also singles out one individual" - A second valid feature, the written label, tied to how the scroll presents individual service.
   - "stone defensive wall built along Hakata Bay in Kyushu" - A specific, accurate development from the period. It is clearly connected to why the 1281 invasion failed. Earns the point.
   - "exposed when a typhoon struck and destroyed much of it" - The storm is tied to the 1281 fleet and linked to the Japanese defenses, which is what stronger answers do.
   - "Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260" - Names a specific state and an accurate event. The similarity is explained, since both states resisted and defeated the Mongols. Earns the point.
   - "Japan was protected partly because the Mongols had to cross the sea" - An accurate difference that adds depth to the comparison.

This refusal helps explain why the Mongols sent the invasion fleets, because Kublai Khan wanted Japan to recognize him as ruler and he saw the refusal as a challenge to his power.

(C) Japan's experience with the Mongols was different from other places because the Mongols were a really big threat everywhere and a lot of countries had a hard time against them. a: The image shows the Japanese warriors as armored horsemen carrying bows and full quivers of arrows, presenting them as skilled mounted archers ready for battle.
The warriors are shown riding together as a group through pine trees, presenting them as an organized force moving into action rather than as individuals at rest.

The column of writing at the top names a particular warrior, so the image presents the defense against the Mongols in terms of one man's individual service, fitting a scroll commissioned by Takezaki Suenaga to record his service.
The warriors wear elaborate colored armor and helmets, presenting them as well-equipped members of a professional warrior class.
b: Kublai Khan, who founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271, sent envoys demanding that Japan submit and pay tribute; the Kamakura shogunate under the regent Hojo Tokimune refused, which led to the invasions.
After the 1274 attack, the Kamakura shogunate had warriors build a stone defensive wall along Hakata Bay in Kyushu, which helped prevent the 1281 invasion force from establishing itself on land.

The Mongols relied on ships and conscripted crews from Goryeo Korea, which had submitted to them, and from the conquered Southern Song, showing how they used the resources of subject peoples to attempt a seaborne campaign.
In 1281 a powerful storm wrecked much of the Mongol invasion fleet off Kyushu, which together with Japanese resistance caused the invasion to fail.
c: Similarity: like Japan, the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt successfully stopped Mongol expansion, defeating a Mongol army at Ain Jalut in 1260.
Similarity: like Japan, Dai Viet under the Tran dynasty repelled repeated Mongol invasions, including a victory at the Bach Dang River in 1288.
Difference: unlike Japan, the Song dynasty in China was conquered by Kublai Khan's forces, with Song resistance ending in 1279, and China came under Yuan rule.
Difference: unlike Japan, Goryeo Korea eventually submitted to the Mongols after years of resistance and became a subordinate state whose ships and men were used in the invasions of Japan.

common_pitfalls: Identifying the riders in the detail as Mongol soldiers.
Describing parts of the scroll not shown in this detail.
Claiming the artist or Suenaga painted scenes he personally watched, rather than saying the scroll was commissioned to record his service.
Treating the storm as the only reason the invasions failed and ignoring Japanese defenses.
In (c), naming a state but not making an actual comparison with Japan, or choosing an example outside 1200 to 1300.
In (b), simply restating that invasions happened in 1274 and 1281.
facts: Takezaki Suenaga, a warrior from Higo province in Kyushu, commissioned the Moko Shurai Ekotoba around 1293 to record his service against the Mongol invasions.
The Mongol invasions of Japan took place in 1274 and 1281 and both failed.
Kublai Khan proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and completed the conquest of the Southern Song in 1279.
Japan was governed by the Kamakura shogunate, with Hojo Tokimune serving as regent during the invasions.
A stone defensive wall was built along Hakata Bay after the 1274 invasion.
A storm destroyed much of the 1281 invasion fleet.
The Mamluks defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260.
Baghdad was sacked by Mongol forces in 1258, ending the Abbasid Caliphate there.
Dai Viet defeated Mongol forces at the Bach Dang River in 1288.

samples.essay:
(A) The image presents the Japanese warriors as armored horsemen carrying bows and quivers full of arrows, riding together as a group through the pine trees. This shows them as skilled mounted archers ready for battle. The column of writing at the top naming a warrior also singles out one individual, which presents the warriors as men whose personal service deserved to be recorded, fitting the fact that Takezaki Suenaga had the scroll made to show his own deeds.

(B) After the first invasion in 1274, the Kamakura shogunate had a stone defensive wall built along Hakata Bay in Kyushu. When the much larger Yuan fleet arrived in 1281, the wall kept many of the invaders from getting a solid foothold on shore, so they had to stay on their ships for weeks. This left the fleet exposed when a typhoon struck and destroyed much of it, which the Japanese later called the kamikaze, or "divine wind," and the invasion failed.

(C) Japan's experience was similar to that of the Mamluk Sultanate in Egypt, because both states refused to submit to the Mongols and managed to defeat them. The Mamluks beat a Mongol army at the Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260, which stopped the Ilkhanate from moving into Egypt, just as Japan's defenders and the storms stopped the Yuan from conquering Japan. One difference is that the Mamluks won a land battle against Mongol cavalry, while Japan was protected partly because the Mongols had to cross the sea, where their usual strengths mattered less.
